newsitem.title: USA: U.S. alloy braced for GM strike fallout.
newsitem.headline: U.S. alloy braced for GM strike fallout.

text.p: The U.S. aluminum alloy market is braced for the fallout from General Motors Corp's strike if the dispute continues for a week or so longer, industry executives said.

GM is a major consumer of components made by diecasters from secondary aluminum or alloy. The carmaker said Monday that 4,250 of its U.S. employees had been laid off as a result of the Canadian Auto Workers union strike at the company's Canadian plants since October 3.

Midwest alloy smelters said the situation was not precarious yet, but could be given another week to ten days of strikes and continued weak prices for aluminum on the London Metal Exchange, aluminum scrap would start to be freed up.
"We will inevitably start seeing some effects and potential slowdown as far as our alloy shipments are concerned if it continues much longer," the executive said.
An East coast smelter official added, "We are getting ready for it - I have a feeling we will see some cheap selling this week."

Alloy prices in the Midwest are languishing around 63 cents per pound delivered consumer's works. "If we see a continued GM strike relative to what happens on LME, it potentially might go lower," the executive added.
LME primary aluminum, a major factor in alloy prices, have just off two and a half year lows. LME alloy contract cash settled Monday at 53.5 cents per pound in warehouse.
Scrap prices have already tumbled a couple of cents in the past week while A380 grade alloy has remained about 63 cents though some believed that 62 cents was closer to the market.
Copper scrap merchants said they saw no significant signs yet of any requests for delays in scrap shipments due to the GM strike.
